data.name: Tipaw

audit.sub: Where the account is leaking, and where the upside is. All figures Klaviyo-attributed unless noted; windows are the last 3 / 6 / 12 complete months through Jun 2026. The latest month (Jul) is month-to-date, shown faded and marked *.
audit.title: Account audit

findings.body: New subscribers climbed from ~1,200/mo a year ago to 7,100+/mo (about 6x; ~4.7x on a 3-month-average basis). Flow revenue grew too, but only about 2.7x. We would not expect it to keep pace one-for-one: scaling paid acquisition pulls in lower-intent subscribers, so revenue per subscriber naturally softens. But even on a conservative diminishing-returns basis (the dashed line, set halfway between full efficiency and where they sit today), a well-run lifecycle should be pulling roughly €32k/mo at this audience size versus the ~€25k it is doing. That gap runs about €7k/mo on a 3-month average and is widening (near €12k in June): recoverable flow revenue the lifecycle is leaving on the table as the audience scales. Toggle to List vs revenue: subscribers and automation revenue are each indexed to 100 at the start of the window. Tipaw's subscriber count grew about 5x while automation revenue grew only about 2.8x, so revenue is falling behind the list. In our longest-managed client the reverse holds: revenue grew about 2.7x against about 1.5x subscriber growth, so each new subscriber is worth more, not less.
findings.title: List growth is outrunning the lifecycle

findings.body: This is finding 1 seen per email rather than in total. As the audience scaled, revenue per recipient (€/Rec, revenue per individual email delivered) fell from about 0.61 to 0.31, nearly halved, while flow send volume doubled (37k to 74k/mo). Some softening is expected: a bigger, colder audience converts less per send, so we would not hold €/Rec flat. But even allowing for that (the dashed target, the same diminishing-returns basis as finding 1), a well-run program should sit near 0.47 per recipient at this volume, not 0.31. Closing that gap is worth roughly €12k/mo at the current send volume, the same money as finding 1, expressed per email.
findings.title: Send volume doubled, revenue per recipient (€/Rec) nearly halved

findings.body: The Welcome flow alone drives 57% of flow revenue, and it is a sprawling 21-live-email flow. Even a well-run account leans on Welcome, but our longest-managed client keeps its top flow near 40% with a fuller mid-tail: more flows each pulling real revenue. Tipaw is over-concentrated. Strengthening Cart, Checkout, Post-Purchase and Winback so no single flow carries half the automated revenue is the fix. Flow names link straight to each flow; the tick on each bar (and the column) shows the same-rank flow at the benchmark.
findings.title: 57% of automated revenue rides on one flow

findings.body: Several flows re-open too slowly, or not at all, leaving repeat revenue on the table. Abandonment flows re-open only after 30 to 60 days (should be 4 to 7), so a repeat abandoner never re-enters. Review requests re-open after 180 days (should be within 30) and the post-review flow is enter-once (should re-open after about 7 days). The post-purchase flows are effectively order and shipping confirmations: Shopify sends its own, but customers like the reassurance that we have their order and it is on the way, so these should re-open after about 3 days rather than enter-once, so repeat buyers get them on every order. Welcome (once) and Winback (yearly) are set sensibly. Red rows re-open too slowly; names link to each flow. These are fast, low-risk changes with immediate upside.
findings.title: Abandonment flows re-open far too slowly (money left on the table)

findings.body: The blended rate hides the real driver. Broken out, flow unsub rate runs about 1.0% (0.9-1.1%), roughly double the campaign rate (~0.5%) and 3-4x a healthy target (~0.2-0.3%). Drilling into the last 90 days, the churn concentrates in a handful of emails: the first Welcome email loses subscribers at ~1.8%, and several Welcome and Product Abandonment emails run 1.1-2.0%. Toggle Blended to combine the lines; expand the list below to see the worst offender emails, each linked to open in Klaviyo.
findings.title: Flow unsubscribe rate is the churn engine (about double campaigns)

findings.body: Email drove 28.7% of total store revenue over 12 months but only 25.8% over the last 3, dipping toward 24% recently, even as the store scaled from about €89k/mo to €140k/mo. Scaling does not require that. The dashed line is our longest-managed client over the same 12 months: as its store scaled, its email share climbed from about 27% to 40%. A well-run lifecycle gains share as the business grows, it does not cede it.
findings.title: Email's share of revenue is slipping as the store scales

findings.body: No flow or campaign sends SMS, yet the account is actively collecting SMS subscribers. Opt-ins switched on around February 2026 and have climbed to about 2,717 a month, roughly 6,465 gathered in the last year and still rising. So there is a growing, contactable SMS list being built and paid for, with zero sends against it. Toggle the growth chart in finding 1 to SMS to watch the list climb. For abandonment and winback in particular, SMS drives strong incremental revenue: this is a channel already half-built and left completely idle.
findings.title: SMS: a growing subscriber list, zero sends

findings.body: Several proven flows simply do not exist. There is no Back-in-Stock flow, so whenever a popular item sells out, demand at the exact moment of intent goes uncaptured. There is no Birthday flow to capture a customer's, or their pet's, birthday, a fun, high-open moment to re-engage the audience. There is no first-purchase bounce-back to turn a first-time buyer into a second order while intent is highest. And there is no VIP series to recognise and reward the true believers, the small group of best customers who drive most repeat revenue. Each of these is a standard, high-return part of a mature lifecycle. The flows that do exist are thin on the retention side: post-purchase returns just 0.20 to 0.28 per email and Winback 0.34. Repeat-purchase and re-engagement revenue is underbuilt.
findings.title: High-value flows that are missing entirely

findings.body: Ordered by send volume, with revenue per recipient shown per flow. Product (browse) Abandonment is the second-biggest sender at 87,557 emails, yet returns just 0.15 per recipient and a 0.24% order rate, far below Cart (0.61) and Checkout (1.51). Browse is lower-intent by nature, but this much volume at this return drags overall efficiency and feeds the unsubscribes in card 5. It also runs a live duplicate. Names link to each flow.
findings.title: A high-volume flow is underperforming

findings.body: Subscription management runs in Recharge, which is fine in itself. Recharge is already connected to Klaviyo and streaming the events (subscription started, cancelled, next charge date, charge failed, and more), so the data is right there. The problem is that none of it is used to gate the browse, cart and checkout abandonment flows. As things stand, an active subscriber who is simply browsing can be dropped into an abandonment flow and pushed to buy something they already receive on a schedule: a poor experience that can even prompt a cancellation. The fix is to translate Recharge subscription status into Klaviyo and suppress abandonment for active subscribers, and ideally to bring the core subscription lifecycle (upcoming charge, failed payment, win back a cancel) into Klaviyo so it sits inside the ESP alongside everything else. Keeping it in Recharge is also fine; either way the data needs to be wired in properly. This is exactly the ESP-plus-subscription-SaaS integration we handle routinely, and giving the ESP what it does best consistently lifts results.
findings.title: Subscriptions run through Recharge, but the flows do not use it

findings.body: The 'Triple Pixel (2)' flows are identity-resolution (IDR) versions of the four abandonment flows: they recover visitors whose tracking cookies have dehydrated, so more abandoners still receive an email. That is a smart setup worth keeping. One refinement: Triple Pixel is among the less reliable IDR tools (it ships free with Triple Whale, which may be why it is in place). It is worth trialing a stronger provider, such as Aimerce, against it to see how many more identities, and how much more abandonment revenue, the same traffic can recover.
findings.title: Identity resolution is running on the abandonment flows (good, but the provider is worth upgrading)

findings.body: No experiments or A/B tests have been run in this account, at any point. That is the root cause behind the earlier findings: as paid acquisition scaled, revenue per recipient fell (card 2) and email's share of revenue slipped (card 6), because nothing in the lifecycle is being improved to keep pace with a larger, colder audience. Our longest-serving accounts compound the other way: we ship new creative and test relentlessly, so revenue per recipient rises with the brand instead of falling. Losing tests are cut fast; every winner becomes the new baseline until it is beaten, so improvements bank permanently. Even a 10% win rate would pay off, and ours is a 67% global win rate, and climbing, because a central brain compounds learnings from every test across every account.
findings.title: Zero A/B testing: the lifecycle is not learning

findings.body: Everything in this audit is day-to-day work for us: the testing engine, the flow architecture, the list health, the channel expansion, the integrations. The findings above are the roadmap, and the testing engine in finding 12 is what turns each fix into a compounding gain rather than a one-off. Most of our clients sit between $3M and $20M in revenue, with the average around $5M to $8M, but we also work with smaller budgets. We build a package to fit: a baseline of what we typically do, scaled up or down to match where you are.
findings.title: Where Zee.Media comes in
